title: Wheat Leaf Rust (Puccinia triticina)
content: Wheat leaf rust (Puccinia triticina) is one of the most widespread and destructive fungal diseases of wheat. Symptoms include small, circular to oval, orange-brown pustules scattered on the upper leaf surface. The disease thrives in temperatures of 15-22°C with high humidity. Management: Use resistant varieties (e.g., Faisalabad-085, Lasani-085). Apply fungicides like propiconazole (Tilt 250EC) at 0.5L/acre when disease severity reaches 5-10%. Early sowing (November) reduces rust incidence. Remove volunteer wheat plants that serve as green bridge hosts.

title: Cotton Bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera)
content: Cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) is the most damaging pest of cotton in Pakistan. Larvae bore into bolls causing direct yield loss of 20-40%. Symptoms: bore holes in bolls with frass, damaged squares and flowers. Monitoring: Use pheromone traps (5 traps/acre). Economic threshold: 10 eggs or 5 larvae per plant. Management: Plant Bt cotton varieties. Release Trichogramma parasitoids at 50,000/acre. Apply neem-based pesticides (Azadirachtin 1500ppm) at 2.5ml/L. Chemical control: Emamectin benzoate (Proclaim 5SG) at 200g/acre or Chlorantraniliprole (Coragen 20SC) at 100ml/acre. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides to preserve natural enemies.

title: Rice Blast Disease (Magnaporthe oryzae)
document_title: Rice Disease Management Guide for Pakistan
content: Rice blast (Magnaporthe oryzae) affects leaves, nodes, and panicles. Leaf symptoms: diamond-shaped lesions with gray centers and brown borders, typically 1-1.5cm long. Node blast causes stem breakage. Panicle blast (neck blast) causes empty or partially filled grains. Favored by: temperatures 20-25°C, high humidity (>90%), excessive nitrogen, dense planting. Management: Use resistant varieties (Super Basmati, KS-282). Balanced NPK fertilizer (avoid excess nitrogen). Maintain proper plant spacing (20x20cm). Drain fields periodically. Fungicide: Tricyclazole (Beam 75WP) at 150g/acre or Isoprothiolane (Fuji-one 40EC) at 500ml/acre at early disease appearance.

title: Citrus Canker (Xanthomonas citri)
content: Citrus canker (Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri) causes raised, corky lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit. Leaf lesions: 3-10mm, raised, crater-like with water-soaked margins. Fruit lesions: corky, cratered, reduce market value. Spread by wind-driven rain, contaminated tools, and infected nursery stock. Management: Use certified disease-free nursery plants. Prune and destroy infected branches (disinfect tools with 10% bleach). Copper-based sprays: Bordeaux mixture (1%) or Copper oxychloride (3g/L) at 15-day intervals during rainy season. Windbreaks reduce spread. Avoid overhead irrigation. Quarantine new orchard plants for 6 months.

title: Sugarcane Red Rot (Colletotrichum falcatum)
content: Sugarcane red rot (Colletotrichum falcatum) causes drying of the crown and midrib, with internal reddening of the cane. External symptoms: drying of leaves from the tip downward, reddish discoloration of midribs, white patches on the rind. Internal: pith becomes reddish-brown with white patches, sour smell. Severe losses in ratoon crops. Management: Use disease-free seed cane (setts). Hot water treatment of setts (52°C for 30 minutes). Plant resistant varieties (HSF-240, CPF-246). Avoid waterlogging. Rogue out diseased clumps early. Three-tier seed production system. Crop rotation with non-host crops (wheat, berseem) for 2-3 years in affected fields.

title: Tomato Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
content: Tomato late blight (Phytophthora infestans) causes water-soaked lesions on leaves that turn brown-black. Under humid conditions, white fuzzy growth appears on leaf undersides. Stems develop dark brown lesions. Fruit shows firm, greasy-looking brown lesions. Disease spreads rapidly in cool (18-22°C), wet conditions. Management: Plant resistant/tolerant varieties (Roma VF, Rio Grande). Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation. Stake plants for better air circulation. Remove and destroy infected plant debris. Preventive sprays: Mancozeb (Dithane M-45) at 2g/L at 7-10 day intervals during humid weather. Curative: Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold MZ) at 2.5g/L at first symptom appearance.

title: Mango Sudden Death Syndrome (Ceratocystis fimbriata)
content: Mango sudden death syndrome (Ceratocystis fimbriata) causes rapid wilting and death of mango trees within 2-4 weeks. Symptoms: gummosis (amber-colored gum exuding from trunk), bark splitting, internal wood discoloration (brown to black streaks), sudden leaf wilting and browning. Spread by root grafting, contaminated irrigation water, and pruning tools. Management: No effective cure once tree is infected. Prevention: Use disease-free nursery stock from certified nurseries. Avoid flood irrigation (use drip/basin). Do not intercrop with susceptible plants. Disinfect tools between trees. Remove and burn infected trees including roots. Soil treatment: Trichoderma harzianum (10g/L) drench around healthy trees as preventive measure. Copper oxychloride (3g/L) trunk paint.

title: Wheat Aphid Management (Sitobion avenae)
content: Wheat aphids (Sitobion avenae, Rhopalosiphum padi) suck plant sap and transmit Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV). Heavy infestation causes yellowing, stunted growth, and 15-30% yield loss. Monitoring: Check 20 plants at 5 locations per field. Economic threshold: 10-15 aphids per tiller during boot stage. Natural enemies: Ladybird beetles, syrphid flies, parasitoid wasps (Aphidius colemani). Management: Early sowing (by Nov 15) avoids peak aphid populations. Conserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides. Chemical control (only above threshold): Imidacloprid (Confidor 200SL) at 50ml/acre or Thiamethoxam (Actara 25WG) at 50g/acre. Spray at booting stage, avoid flowering period to protect pollinators.

title: Potato Late Blight Management
document_title: Potato Production and Protection in South Asia
content: Potato late blight (Phytophthora infestans) is the most devastating potato disease. Leaf symptoms: irregular, water-soaked pale green lesions that turn brown-black. White mold on leaf undersides in humid weather. Tubers develop firm, brown, irregular lesions on skin; internal flesh shows reddish-brown granular rot. Favored by 10-24°C with >90% humidity for 10+ hours. Management: Use certified disease-free seed tubers. Plant resistant varieties (Asterix, Diamant). Hill up soil to protect tubers. Avoid overhead irrigation late in the day. Harvest only when foliage is completely dry and dead. Curing tubers at 15-18°C for 10-14 days before storage. Fungicides: Chlorothalonil (Daconil 75WP) at 2g/L preventively; Cymoxanil+Mancozeb (Curzate M-8) at 2.5g/L curatively. Alternate fungicide groups to prevent resistance.

title: Maize Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
document_title: Fall Armyworm Management in South Asia
content: Fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) is an invasive pest causing 30-70% yield loss in maize. Larvae feed on leaves (windowpane damage), whorls, and ears. Identification: inverted Y on head, four dots forming a square on the last body segment. Most damaging in seedling to tasseling stages. Monitoring: Pheromone traps, check whorls for frass and larvae. Management: Early planting synchronized with community. Hand-pick and destroy egg masses and larvae in small fields. Apply sand+lime mixture (9:1) into whorls. Biological: Nuclear polyhedrosis virus (NPV) at 250LE/ha, Trichogramma releases. Chemical (economic threshold: 5% plants infested): Chlorantraniliprole (Coragen 20SC) at 100ml/acre, Emamectin benzoate (Proclaim 5SG) at 200g/acre, or Spinetoram (Delegate 120SC) at 100ml/acre directed into whorl. Rotate insecticide groups.

title: Chili Leaf Curl Virus (ChiLCV)
content: Chili leaf curl virus (ChiLCV) transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) causes upward curling of leaves, thickened veins, stunted growth, and reduced fruit set. Yield losses of 30-80% in severe cases. Disease severity peaks during warm, dry weather with high whitefly populations. Management: Use virus-resistant/tolerant varieties (Longi, Wonder Hot, Skyline). Raise seedlings under insect-proof nets (50 mesh). Yellow sticky traps (12/acre) for whitefly monitoring. Neem oil (2ml/L) sprays for whitefly repellence. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately (rogueing). Chemical whitefly control: Diafenthiuron (Pegasus 500SC) at 300ml/acre or Pyriproxyfen (Admiral 10EC) at 250ml/acre. Avoid monocrotophos and other broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural enemies.

title: Onion Purple Blotch (Alternaria porri)
content: Onion purple blotch (Alternaria porri) causes elliptical, purple-centered lesions on leaves and flower stalks. Lesions enlarge, coalesce, and cause leaf dieback from tips. Severe infection reduces bulb size by 30-50%. Favored by warm (25-30°C), humid conditions and prolonged leaf wetness. Management: Use healthy, certified seed. Seed treatment with Carbendazim (2g/kg seed). Wider spacing (15x10cm) for air circulation. Avoid excess nitrogen. Drip irrigation to minimize leaf wetness. Fungicide: Mancozeb (2g/L) or Iprodione (Rovral 50WP, 2g/L) at 10-day intervals from first symptoms. Harvest when 50% tops have fallen. Cure bulbs at 30-35°C for 7-10 days before storage. Proper ventilation in storage.

title: Banana Panama Disease (Fusarium wilt)
content: Banana Panama disease (Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense) causes vascular wilting. Symptoms: yellowing of older leaves progressing upward, splitting of leaf bases, internal vascular discoloration (brown-black streaks), and plant collapse. Tropical Race 4 (TR4) is the most threatening strain. Management: Use disease-free tissue-cultured plantlets. Quarantine new planting material. Do not replant bananas in infected soil for 20+ years. Flood fallowing for 6+ months. Biological control: Trichoderma harzianum-enriched compost. Resistant varieties: GCTCV-218, GCTCV-119. Soil drenching with Carbendazim (1g/L) provides limited control. Strict farm hygiene: footbaths, vehicle disinfection, no sharing of farm tools between fields. Remove and destroy infected plants including corms.

title: Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus (YVMV)
content: Okra yellow vein mosaic virus (YVMV) causes bright yellow veins, interveinal chlorosis, leaf curling, and stunted growth. Transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Severe during summer (May-September) with yield losses up to 50%. Management: Use tolerant varieties (Pusa Sawani, Arka Anamika, Sabz Pari). Raise nursery under net house. Plant marigold as border crop to repel whiteflies. Yellow sticky traps (10-12/acre). Rogue infected plants early. Neem seed kernel extract (5%) sprays every 10 days. Whitefly chemical control: Thiamethoxam (Actara 25WG) at 50g/acre. Reflective mulch (silver) repels whiteflies. Avoid ratooning of okra crops. Crop rotation with non-host crops (cereals) for one season.

title: Groundnut Leaf Spot (Cercospora personata)
content: Groundnut late leaf spot (Cercospora personata) causes dark brown to black circular spots (2-5mm) on leaves with yellow halos. Severe infection causes premature defoliation, reducing yield by 20-50%. Favored by warm (25-30°C), humid weather. Management: Use resistant/tolerant varieties (BARI-2011, BARD-479). Crop rotation with cereals for 2-3 years. Deep plowing after harvest to bury crop debris. Seed treatment with Thiram (3g/kg) or Carbendazim (2g/kg). Foliar spray: Chlorothalonil (2g/L) or Hexaconazole (Contaf 5EC, 2ml/L) starting at first symptoms at 10-15 day intervals. Timely harvesting when 75% pods show dark internal shell color.
